title: Maximum White Tiles Covered By A Carpet
description:
You are given a 2D array `tiles` where `tiles[i] = [l_i, r_i]` means every integer position from `l_i` to `r_i` (inclusive) is a **white** tile. The ranges do not overlap, but they are **not** necessarily given in sorted order. Every position not covered by a range is not white.

You also have one carpet that covers exactly `carpetLen` consecutive integer positions, and you may place it starting at any integer position.

Return the maximum number of white tiles the carpet can cover.

**Example 1:**
```
Input: tiles = [[2,6],[9,10],[14,20],[23,24]], carpetLen = 8
Output: 7
Explanation: Place the carpet on positions 14 through 21. It covers the whole range 14-20, which is 7 white tiles. No other placement of length 8 covers more.
```

**Example 2:**
```
Input: tiles = [[15,17],[3,4],[8,9]], carpetLen = 3
Output: 3
Explanation: Placing the carpet on positions 15-17 covers 3 white tiles. The ranges are not necessarily given in sorted order.
```

**Example 3:**
```
Input: tiles = [[2,4],[7,9]], carpetLen = 6
Output: 4
Explanation: Positions 2-7 cover tiles 2, 3, 4 and 7, i.e. 4 white tiles. No placement of length 6 covers more, because the gap 5-6 always lies inside any window that touches both ranges.
```

examples.explanation: Place the carpet on positions 14 through 21. It covers the whole range 14-20, which is 7 white tiles. No other placement of length 8 covers more.
Placing the carpet on positions 15-17 covers 3 white tiles. The ranges are not necessarily given in sorted order.
Positions 2-7 cover tiles 2, 3, 4 and 7, i.e. 4 white tiles. No placement of length 6 covers more, because the gap 5-6 always lies inside any window that touches both ranges.

constraints: The ranges in tiles are pairwise non-overlapping
solution_approach: A brute force tries every starting position and counts covered white cells, which is far too slow since coordinates reach 10^9. Key observation: some optimal placement starts at the left end of a tile range (sliding a carpet right until its start hits a range start never loses tiles). So sort the ranges, build prefix sums of range lengths, and for each range i place the carpet at [l_i, l_i + carpetLen - 1]. Binary search the last range j whose start is <= the carpet end; the covered count is the full lengths of ranges i..j-1 (from prefix sums) plus the partial overlap of range j, min(r_j, end) - l_j + 1. A two-pointer sliding window replaces the binary search with the same idea. Time is O(n log n) and space O(n).
hints: Coordinates are huge, so you cannot simulate every position. Where is it always safe to start the carpet?
An optimal carpet can always be aligned to start at the left end of some white range. Sort the ranges and consider only those n starting points.
With prefix sums of range lengths, binary search the last range starting at or before l_i + carpetLen - 1; add the fully covered ranges plus the partial overlap of that last range.
follow_up_questions: How would you handle the case where the input ranges may overlap?
What if you had two carpets that cannot overlap each other?
